en: Chapter 1:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiation for the law of Yama;
one should prescribe expiation for all four castes as well. (YS 1.1)
But a Brahmin who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal,
or a wolf shall become pure immediately upon seeing the rising of a planet or a constellation.
Those who have perished by water, fire, or hanging; those who have fallen from the religious life or through fasting unto death;
those whose bodies have been struck by poison or serpents; and those who have been killed by the blow of weapons.
These nine, having fallen away and being excluded from all religious duties,
are purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and by two Taptakṛcchra penances.
Those wicked ones who have fallen from both [paths] and are mottled by tranquility are purified by giving a cow and likewise a bull, as if by two moons.
If one has killed, burned, or caused the death by hanging a cow or a Brahmin,
one should cut the noose and then perform two *taptakṛcchra* penances.
If [the food] is infested with worms or contaminated by flies,
one should perform half a *kṛcchra* penance and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability.
Having drunk water that has touched a Cāṇḍāla’s vessel or water that has reached the ground,
one becomes pure after six nights by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel.
If a twice-born man drinks water contained in a jar belonging to a Caṇḍāla,
he becomes pure by performing the Prājāpatya penance if he discards it at that very moment.
If one does not discharge water [as urine] and yet his body undergoes digestion,
the Prājāpatya penance, as well as the Kṛcchra, Sāṃtapana, and others, should not be prescribed for him.
A Brahmin should perform the Sāṃtapana penance, while a Kṣatriya should perform the Prājāpatya;
a Vaiśya should perform half of that, and one should cause a Śūdra to perform a quarter of it.
Having consumed the food of a Cāṇḍāla, as well as their water,
a Brāhmaṇa should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one month, or alternatively, the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass,
followed by a fast for one night— this is known as the *sāṃtapana* penance.
Having given food to those who have the form of Cāṇḍālas or those of mixed birth, and having eaten such food oneself, one should perform the Taptakṛcchra penance.
A twice-born man who has sexual intercourse with women of the Cāṇḍāla caste is purified by performing the Aghamarṣaṇa rite for half a month and by observing a vow of consuming only milk.
Thus ends the first chapter in the glorious Yāmya Dharmaśāstra.
Having approached an actress, a dancer, a washerwoman, a basket-weaver,
or one who lives by working with skins, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (YS 2.1)
For those who eat the food of Kāpālikas or who approach their daughters, a Kṛcchra penance is prescribed if done unknowingly; if done knowingly, two vows are required.
If a Brahmin has consumed liquor or eaten beef, he shall perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance; he is purified by the *mauñjī-homa*.
Having specifically recognized a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra born in the natural order (anuloma), one should then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
One should take a morsel of food the size of a hen’s egg;
otherwise, due to the fault of improper disposition, one is purified on the ninth day.
One should increase the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight;
on the new moon day, however, one should not eat at all—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
If the performer dies after having begun the penance,
he becomes purified by that [penance] both in this world and in the next.
As long as even one person remains separate and does not undergo penance,
they are all unworthy, untouchable, and censured.
Those who are unfit to be fed with, unfit to receive gifts from, unfit to sit in a row at a meal, and unfit to marry into—
these are all purified once the vow has been performed, and they shall share in the inheritance.
Thus ends the second chapter in the glorious Dharmaśāstra of Yama.
For one who is less than eleven years of age and more than five years old,
the brother, the father, or another relative shall perform the penance. (YS 3.1)
Therefore, even for one who is most ignorant, there is neither offense nor sin;
he incurs no royal punishment, nor is there any need for expiation.
A child over eighty years of age, or one under sixteen,
as well as women and those who are ill, deserve only half of the prescribed penance.
One should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance for having sexual intercourse with the wife of a paternal uncle, the wife of a brother, one’s own sister, a mother-in-law, or a father’s sister.
Having approached out of delusion these women— the queen, the wife of a teacher or a disciple, or the wife of a preceptor— one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for six months.
For two months he should subsist on solid and soft foods; for two months on barley-gruel;
for two months on the five products of the cow; and for six months he should perform the kṛcchra penance.
Having approached his mother, the wife of his guru, a sister, or likewise a daughter, he shall enter the fire; no other purification is prescribed.
When the sun has set, if someone should touch a Caṇḍāla or a woman in her menses,
what should the expiation be?
Having bathed with gold or silver, or with water brought during the day,
and having drunk it and touched a cow, one becomes purified.
Slaves, potters, cowherds, family friends, and those who cultivate half the land—
these Śūdras may have their food eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Those ignorant twice-born ones who eat food from Śūdras,
having incurred the need for atonement, should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
If a twice-born man commits the act of consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that [sin] by constantly reciting [the mantra] during meals for three years.
But that Brahmin who, deluded by intoxication, takes a *vṛṣalī* as his wife,
is perpetually tainted by the state of being born from a *sūta* (the offspring of a Kṣatriya father and Brāhmaṇa mother), and incurs the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa day after day.
Furthermore, by having continuous sexual intercourse with a *vṛṣalī* for one month,
one becomes a *śūdra* in this very life and will subsequently become a dog.
For one who has drunk the saliva of a *vṛṣalī*, for one who has been approached by her breath,
and for one who has begotten a child upon her, no expiation is prescribed.
Having seen a buffalo-slaughterer at the beginning, a husband of a low-caste woman in the middle,
and a usurer at the end, the ancestors departed in despair.
A wife is called a *mahiṣī*, and she may indeed be unfaithful;
he who endures those faults is known as a *māhiṣaka*.
If a maiden in her father’s house sees her menses while remaining uninitiated with the marriage rite, her father incurs the sin of killing an embryo; such a maiden is declared to be a *vṛṣalī*.
That Brahmin who, deluded by intoxication, marries such a girl is unfit for conversation and excluded from the ritual row; he is a Brahmin who is the husband of a Vṛṣalī.
When the twelfth year has arrived, he who does not give away his daughter—
month after month, her father drinks her menstrual blood.
A girl of eight years is Gaurī, one of nine years is Rohiṇī, and one of ten years is Kanyā; beyond this age, she is Rajasvalā (menstruating).
The mother, the father, and likewise the elder brother—
these three go to hell upon seeing a girl who has reached her menses.
He who, having discarded wealth that is of moderate value, bestows that which is of great value,
is indeed to be known as a usurer, and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
A barren woman who causes the depletion of semen is declared to be one who should be abandoned;
one should know her husband to be like a goat or a sheep.
He who eats without honoring a Brahmin who has come to his house from afar, exhausted and overcome by fear, is at that very moment transformed [into a dog].
One who keeps goats and sheep, one who keeps buffaloes, and likewise the husband of a Śūdra woman,
having been touched even by the tip of a blade of grass [from them], shall enter the water with their clothes on.
As long as the food remains warm, as long as they eat in silence,
and as long as the qualities of the oblation are not mentioned, for so long do the ancestors partake of it.
The qualities of the sacrificial offering should not be mentioned while the ancestors remain unsatisfied;
once the ancestors have been satisfied, one may subsequently say that the offering was excellent.
As many mouthfuls as one who is uninvited eats at offerings to the gods or ancestors,
so many glowing, iron-made mouthfuls shall he eat after death.
One should offer a seat to those who have seats, but never to those who do not; for if one offers a seat to those who have no seats, the ancestors depart disappointed.
If a twice-born man eats while having his foot placed upon a seat, with half of his garment tucked down, or blowing on the food with his mouth, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
He who, having placed the purifiers on his finger, should offer perfumes, does not reach the ancestors; he is plundered by Rākṣasas.

He who eats with a full mouthful, makes noise while eating, eats with a slurping sound, licks his fingers, rolls his food into balls, and [eats with his mouth open]— these six are defilers of the row.

One who has white leprosy, one with skin disease, one suffering from colic, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who is diseased, one with missing or extra limbs, a slanderer, and likewise one who is envious; (these are excluded).
For one who is unfortunate, a eunuch, a heretic, a reviler of the Vedas, a sophist, a priest for Śūdras, and a sacrificer for those who should not be sacrificed for— these are likewise excluded.

One who is constantly greedy for receiving gifts, a beggar, one whose nature is centered on sense-objects, one with black teeth, a physician, and likewise one who engages in improper conversation; YS 3.36.
These individuals must be avoided with great effort at a funeral rite (śrāddha) and at a gift-giving ceremony (dāna),
as well as the temple-priest (devalaka), the hired laborer, and the seller of the Vedas.
These [persons] should be avoided with effort; thus indeed Yama has declared.
The ancestors of such a person become hopeless and remain bearers of his debt.

"Furthermore, if he is a Vaiṣṇava who is liberated from [the cycle of] mantras and possesses knowledge, he indeed should be employed for the offerings to gods (havya) and ancestors (kavya); so Yama himself has declared. (YS 3.39)
Therefore, with every effort, in the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha), sacrifices, and other rituals,
one should diligently appoint a preeminent Brahmin who is beyond reproach.
In the same way, one who is free from the bodily defects that defile a row and is endowed with the knowledge of mantras— Yama has declared that such a person is indeed a purifier of the row.
Free from envy, of virtuous conduct, learned in the Vedas, young, a knower of Brahman, endowed with learning and humility— such is the best of the twice-born, a worthy recipient.

One who knows the Vedānta, who is proficient in the Jyeṣṭhasāman chants, and who is free from greed—such a person, devoted to that [knowledge], should be diligently employed in rites for the gods and the ancestors; for whatever is eaten or offered as an oblation to him becomes infinite. Of this there is no doubt. (YS 3.43)
A twice-born man who has been touched by the leavings of food from a dog or a Śūdra is purified by fasting for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a Brahmin has touched a vessel containing food-leavings that was devoid of food through negligence, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
If a Brāhmaṇa is touched by one who is impure from eating remnants, he should subsequently recite the Daśarudrī; the supreme purification is through the Gāyatrī.
If a dog, a cock, a cat, or a crow should touch one, one becomes pure by fasting for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
"But that twice-born man who has been defiled by the leavings [of food] becomes pure after a day and night;
his purification shall be by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)—so said the blessed Lord Yama."
He who touches a woman in her menses shall observe a three-night penance;
having fasted and performed the purification rite for a twice-born man, he becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow.
Indeed, by the glance of a woman in her courses, or even by hearing her voice,
bathing, worship of the gods, giving, and fire-offerings are rendered null and void.
The seller of red cloth, one who dyes with lac, those who live by bamboo, fishermen, carpenters, and those who subsist on leather; YS 182v 3.52.
By touching these,
as well as by being deluded and accepting gifts from them, a Brahmin indeed goes to hell.
If a Brāhmaṇa, through negligence, touches a woman in her courses,
he becomes pure by fasting for six nights, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Even while impurity (sūtaka) is occurring, what ritual action should be performed by the group of servants?
It is taught that their impurity shall be equal to that of their master.
Yama did not say that one should not cause another to perform [the rite] when such a task has arisen during weddings, festivals, sacrifices, or other similar occasions.
If a woman sees menstrual blood (rajas), what rite should she perform at that time? Having bathed in abundant water, dressed in white garments, and adorned with ornaments— ||| 3.57 ||
One should consecrate [the image] with the verse "āpo hi ṣṭha" or with the verses beginning "āyaṃ gauḥ";
then, at the conclusion of the worship, one should subsequently offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter.
Then one should perform the ritual with the Gāyatrī and the Vyāhṛtis,
as long as the twice-born are not honored with gifts of food, grain, and gold.
Even for one who has observed vows for that long, that sin is not destroyed.
If the body, which is sometimes smeared with the impurities of crows,
cranes, and blue jays, becomes defiled on the ears, the mouth, or the head, purification occurs through bathing for one whose body has been struck by such smearing.
What is the expiation for consuming things that should not be eaten, drunk, or licked, such as semen, urine, and excrement? (YS 182v 3.62)
Having drunk the water of these— lotus, udumbara, bilva, kuśa, aśvattha, and palāśa— one is purified by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If there should be contact with women who are menstruating,
what would be the expiation for members of all four castes?
If women who are menstruating touch one another— whether they belong to the same lineage or different lineages,
and whether it is done intentionally or unintentionally— purification is held to occur after three nights.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former shall perform an Ardha-kṛcchra penance, and the latter likewise a Pāda-kṛcchra.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Vaiśya woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former shall perform a penance reduced by one-quarter, and the latter likewise one quarter.
If a Brāhmaṇī woman and a Śūdra woman touch one another while in their menses,
the Śūdra woman is purified by the Kṛcchra penance, and the Brāhmaṇī woman is purified by giving gifts.
If a Brahmin has been touched at night by a woman in her courses or by an outcaste,
he should bathe with water brought during the day in the presence of fire.
Water touched by the sun during the day, or at night when the stars are visible,
as well as during both twilights, is always pure.
Thus ends the third chapter in the glorious Yāmya Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter 4:
For a dug pond, a large oblong pool, or a well, when [the stone] has been struck by a weapon or even struck by a staff, one should prepare lumps of clay. (YS 182v.4.1)
Whatever sin indeed exists in the killing of a cow or even a bull,
that same expiation shall apply there for either a woman or a man.
A cow that has fallen into a pit, a well, or even a trench overgrown with moss and weeds, or one killed by a blow from a weapon— indeed, such a cow [is not to be eaten].
If a cow, a bull, a calf, or even a young steer should fall or die because of a stick, the man [who caused it] must perform penance.
Whether it be a woman or even a youth, one is purified by means of penance;
a sinner should confess his sin after giving a cow and likewise a bull.
Those who are secret sinners, ungrateful, and of wicked conduct,
are cooked in the hells until the dissolution of all beings.
Therefore, a sinner must undergo penance in whatever manner is appropriate,
especially if he has killed a Kapila cow or any other such animal through negligence.
Just as there is sin in the killing of a Brahmin, so it is in the killing of a Kapila cow;
likewise, the expiation for the killing of a bull is recorded in the tradition as being equal.
Even for one who has killed a cow, purification is attained through penance, whether it be by blocking its path, binding it, or [killing it] with a lump of clay, a blade of grass, or cow dung.
Or a cow struck by a fist, or one running on a cart through water or mud;
cows fallen into a cow-path, or even those crossing a river while being pursued by dogs.
All this has been told to you regarding the supreme destruction of cows,
and the specific expiation for each case where a cow might die.
And if a cow that has fallen in the forest is suspected by a low-caste hunter,
and when that cow dies, he who [suspected her] shall be subject to penance.
Or even if a man has been sent [as a messenger],
whatever penance is prescribed for a Śūdra for a year-long [impurity] shall be double for a Vaiśya.
A cow-slayer must dwell in a cow-pen for three times [the number of days] for a Kṣatriya and four times for a Brāhmaṇa; he must proclaim, "I am a cow-slayer."
Even while living in hardship, one becomes pure through time alone;
one should dwell among cows at night and follow them by day.
One should not perform the shaving of women's heads, nor is it prescribed that they enter a cow-pen;
she should not stay in a cow-pen at night, nor should she recite the Vedic scriptures.
Having raised up all the hair, one should cut it to the length of two finger-breadths;
this alone is recorded as the method for the shaving of the head for women.
O Yama, tell us the rule regarding both birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka);
specifically, what should be done when a birth-impurity is already occurring and a death-impurity also takes place?
"What is that rite prescribed? Tell me exactly as it is.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One Yama spoke according to the truth.
In the case of a birth, there is no doubt that death does not lead to impurity;
however, the previous vow remains unannounced by me, and thus there would be birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Yama himself has declared that one shall not be defiled by birth-impurity;
one shall not be defiled by birth-impurity, and the vow shall reach completion.
Śrāddha rites, charity, austerity, sacrifice, and likewise the propitiation of the deities—
[these do not purify] the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief of gold, and the betrayer of his guru.
The fifth is known as the associate; he is equal to them, there is no doubt in this.
For these [offenses], a penance lasting twelve years is prescribed.
Likewise, for those who have committed mortal sins (pātakin), a penance of six years is prescribed;
and for those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin), a penance of fifteen years is ordained.
By performing three *prājāpatya* penances, one indeed completes a twelve-year *kṛcchra*;
likewise, one may perform a single meal, or eating only at night, or even a full fast.
By means of these four days, the Pādakṛcchra is produced;
the Tripādakṛcchra is to be known as that which is traditionally taught to effect the destruction of sins.
In accordance with the Dharmaśāstras, expiation (prāyaścitta) should be prescribed by the wise for the sake of liberating living beings who have committed sins from their transgressions.
"When remorse indeed arises in sinful men, then an expiation should be granted"; so said the Blessed Lord Yama. (YS 182v_4.28)
He who prescribes an expiation without having understood the treatises on Dharma becomes purified by that expiation himself, while the sin goes to the assembly.
Therefore, atonement is prescribed according to the scriptures for those who have died in a field of eight-row rice, and for those who have died during the birth-impurity of a woman.
Those who have been devoured by fanged beasts, those people who are self-destroyers,
and a Brahmin who has died in Aṣṭaśālī— [for these], an expiation must be performed by their kinsmen.
"One should cause the annual rite and likewise that for women to be performed;
it must not be thought otherwise for the sake of purification," so said the Blessed Lord Yama.
For those who have met with an untimely death or have fallen into a lower state of existence,
two or three years of practice here are indeed recommended for the sake of their purification.
Yama himself has declared that gifts should be given according to the relative gradation of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of the lowest castes.
And for fallen Brahmins as well as for women who have been censured, how may their purification be achieved? Specifically, how may theirs be purified?
There is no doubt that women become pure through menstruation after sexual intercourse;
however, once pregnancy has occurred, there is abandonment [of the child], and not otherwise—this is my teaching.
Merely by seeing a wicked woman, the ancestors go to a downward state;
for she who has gone to another man should have terrible clarified butter poured into her womb.
One should perform the oblation with effort, reciting the Gāyatrī three times ten thousand times,
and afterwards feed one hundred and eight Brahmins.
A widow who consorts with a man must be abandoned by her kinsmen; this is the word of Yama, and not otherwise.
When a fallen brahmin is devoted to remorse and has indeed desisted from evil,
he may then undergo the penance.
When a Brahmin who possesses desire becomes intent on sinful conduct, an expiation must be granted according to the rule, with its degrees of severity.
Having seen [this], one whose flood of sins has been turned back deserves atonement;
likewise do a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra, according to their respective order.
Whatever sin may arise from approaching a widow, whether it occurs once or repeatedly,
once that is known, the expiation is set in motion.
For going [with her] more than once, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
for the sin incurred by going once, it is indeed expiated by two Prājāpatyas.
Indeed, that by which a *punarbhū* (a woman remarried) is made deformed by a Brahmin is called a *punarbhū* even without the formal division of branches [of the Veda]. (YS 182v, 4.45)
And when one who is of the same caste is consecrated as king by another of the same caste,
even if he is a Brahmin, he is censured at śrāddha rites and sacrifices if he is greedy for sensual pleasures.
A Kṣatriya who is attached to a Brāhmaṇī woman, or even to a Vaiśyā woman,
becomes a Śūdra upon approaching a fallen woman, just as you have become.
The wise declare that there is great sin in acting contrary to the natural order;
however, in accordance with the natural order, there is no need for expiation, and otherwise, it is not so.
Mental, verbal, and physical transgressions are recorded as sins;
therefore, for the sake of purification from that evil, one should perform expiation day after day.
One should diligently perform the morning twilight devotion while the stars are still visible;
likewise, the Raudrī at midday and the Vaiṣṇavī in the evening.
The twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) is likewise for the sake of purifying the threefold evil;
for that Brahmin who is devoid of the twilight worship is likewise devoid of ritual bathing.
One who omits bathing becomes a consumer of impurity; one who omits the twilight prayers is indeed a killer of an embryo.
By meditating upon her [the Goddess], one may destroy the sin committed during the night.
For he is intent upon examination. (YS 4.52)
One who is endowed with knowledge and water, being peaceful, pure, and free from desire, goes indeed to the world of Brahmā; it is not otherwise than what Yama has spoken. (YS 4.53)

Those Brahmins who are free from greed, full of joy, and devoid of sin are undoubtedly true gods on earth; they should be known as worthy recipients [of offerings], of this there is no doubt. (YS 182v 4.54)
"Indeed, what is given to them becomes infinite," so said the Blessed Lord Yama;
"but those brahmins who abide in evil deeds, who are greedy, and who are devoid of the Vedas."

What is given to those who have neglected their twilight prayers, who have fallen from their vows, who are malicious, and who are devoted to sensual objects, shall be fruitless; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

When she was restrained by others and became hesitant in accepting gifts, she was released from sin by the sight of the earth; she dwelt upon the boat-like earth during the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages.
"Everything, as well as spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), perishes through the acceptance of gifts from a king;
of this there is no doubt," so said the Blessed Lord Yama.
Those who desire to conquer the three worlds must renounce accepting gifts from kings;
for by accepting gifts from kings, one's status as a Brahmin is indeed destroyed.
Cattle perish by wandering too far; gold, by the desire for greed;
a woman, by pride; and a Brahmin, by service to a king.
And the servants of brahmins and kings are cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells by means of their own good deeds, until the dissolution of all beings.
Those Brahmins who associate with those who should not be associated with, and who act as priests for those for whom one should not perform sacrifices,
are to be known as excluded from the company at meals (apāṅkta) and cast out from all dharma.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the glorious Dharmaśāstra of Yama.
Chapter 5:
Hereafter, O best of sages, listen as I shall proclaim the [rules] for all the outcaste classes and the social orders (varṇas) and so forth, in their proper sequence.
Everything arising from contact with women and so forth is designated as "outcaste" (antyaja);
all that is born of the confusion of wombs is likewise [outcaste] in every respect according to the social classes (varṇa).
Among the castes of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, these [preceding] ones are progressively inferior to the Brāhmaṇa; therefore, the state of being a Brāhmaṇa is supreme.
A Brahmin devoted to Vedic conduct who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences has likewise practiced and specifically expounded that Dharma.
And especially in the performance of their duties, one should be diligent toward those of the three castes;
as well as toward those who have been forcibly enslaved by barbarians, outcastes, or bandits.
If they have committed an impure deed, such as the killing of living beings like cows and so forth,
an expiation must be granted by the twice-born, according to the specific gravity of the offense.
When at the time of a śrāddha ceremony a wife has become menstruating or has given birth,
neither a rite for the gods nor one for the ancestors should be performed.
Whether Brahmins have been consulted or diligently invited,
that rite performed for the sake of the ancestral oblation must indeed be dedicated to the ancestors.
Impurity does not occur at all; there is no need for deliberation on this point, even if his father should pass away while he is on a journey.
But when a funeral rite (śrāddha) and so forth is performed by a son who is unaware [of his father's death], and he hears that his father has died at the time of giving away his daughter; 5.10.
And that gift of the daughter should be performed according to the injunction; it is proper [to do so].
Afterward, all the rites for the father, such as the offering to the vessel and so forth, should be carried out according to the rule.
Whatever has been done out of ignorance— whether pertaining to the gods or to the ancestors— whether at birth or even at death,
all that shall become fruitful.
In the Smṛti composed by Vyāsa himself, it is stated that when the father has died, if he is unknown, the duty should always be performed as if for the father alone.
Even if one has many sons who are indeed united in property,
whatever is performed by the eldest shall result in the entire paternal inheritance being fruitful.

And likewise, everything pertaining to the Vedas certainly comes to pass; there is no doubt regarding the separate funeral ball (*piṇḍa*), the separate *śrāddha* rite, and whatever pertains to the *vaiśvadeva* offering and so forth.
Brothers should perform the rites separately; those who have not divided their property may never do so.
Furthermore, the sons of one who dies without a son shall be the performers of the funeral rites for the sake of the next world.
"Everything becomes fruitful," so said Śātātapa;
"and likewise, even that which has not been given [as a gift] becomes so through great affection. (YS 5.17)
One who has been taken by force, one who has been bound, one given by his kinsmen, the son of a brother, the son of a friend, a disciple, and likewise one who is a biological son (aurasa).
And it should be understood that for one who has no son, these are the heirs; there is no doubt in this matter.
These nine are to be protected like sons, for they indeed bestow the next world.
The portion of Aurasa is known to be equal to that of Vatsoddālaka;
now the sage Śātātapa has declared the determination of the shares.
Whether by the eldest or the youngest, the determination of the partition is made;
and there is no doubt that he who distributes equal shares must give to those who are childless.
Indeed, one who desires a son should always take an equal share from the paternal uncles,
the brothers' sons, and the heirs, in the proper order.
In brief, two shares of the surplus belong to the others;
however, in the case of a mortgage, a gift, or a sale, the prior claim is more powerful.
In all disputes indeed, a stronger subsequent proof prevails;
likewise does a superior argument based on equal knowledge, as well as a counter-objection.
The procedure for deposition is first, and the subsequent [procedure] is fourfold:
when witnesses exist on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff.
When the plaintiff's case has been defeated, the defendants shall prevail;
in legal proceedings where there are no witnesses, an ordeal must be administered according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the glorious Dharmaśāstra of Yama.
This Bṛhadyamasmṛti is completed.
